description:
examples/session_fetch.rs:104 contains:

    println!('state:           {}', session.state);

The Session type has a manual Debug impl (request.rs:212-227) that redacts the state field as '[opaque]' precisely because 'it uniquely identifies the client's session and is the same shape of leak as logging a session cookie' (request.rs:204-206, bd:JMAP-sc1b.99).

State is a String, and {} formatting uses Display (which prints the raw string), bypassing the Debug redaction. The example output to stdout shows the literal state token.

Why this matters: the example is the canonical 'how do I use this crate' reference. A user reading this code learns: 'session.state is fine to log/display.' That is exactly opposite the redaction intent. A user building a JMAP client with logging instrumentation will reach for the example pattern and emit state tokens to their logs.

Workspace AGENTS.md 'Security testing' section #2 set up log-capture canary tests in tests/log_redaction.rs precisely to catch this class of leak through tracing — but that harness doesn't cover example code, and the example reaches around the protection via Display.

Fix options:
1. Add an inline comment near line 104: '// session.state is a session-identifying opaque token; do not log in production'.
2. Replace the line entirely with a placeholder: println!('state:           [opaque]').
3. Print the state's length only: println!('state:           {} bytes', session.state.len()).

Option (1) is the minimum acceptable fix. The example is teaching API usage, and a single comment line at the point of misuse makes the contract visible.
title: examples/session_fetch.rs prints session.state via Display, bypassing the Session Debug redaction
